title: Compute Mastery: From VM to Task
subtitle: Cores, partitions, waves, memory, spill, OOM, autoscaling and the compute decisions behind them
mantra: Workers × cores = slots, partitions = tasks, and no amount of hardware fixes too few partitions, skew or a collect() on the driver.
objectives: You can compute executors, task slots and waves from any compute configuration (driver excluded).
You can explain why partition count, not cluster size, caps a stage's parallelism — and why autoscaling can't fix one partition or skew.
You can reason about scale up vs scale out, memory per core, execution vs storage memory, and spill vs failure.
You can tell driver OOM from executor OOM and walk the memory-debugging chain before adding RAM.
You can name the bottleneck (CPU / memory / I/O / skew) from Spark UI task metrics and pick the matching fix.
You can choose serverless vs classic and Standard vs Dedicated with the selection algorithm, and explain pools, spot, termination and permissions.
You can write spark.conf.get, getNumPartitions, repartition, coalesce and explain('formatted') and know their serverless caveats.
You can dodge the certification traps: executors per worker, zero workers, autoscaling vs instance size, Dedicated ≠ performance, dynamic allocation.

sections.title: What You Buy: The Compute Stack
sections.hook: Look at any compute config and instantly know how many machines, cores and parallel tasks you really have.

blocks.text: **Phase 1 goal**: look at a compute configuration and say *how many machines* you have, *what runs on each*, roughly *how many Spark tasks run at once*, *where OOM can happen*, *how shuffle is affected*, *what autoscaling changes*, and *why serverless or classic*.

blocks.caption: Phase 1 builds from the lowest level up (part 1: the execution hierarchy)
Part 2: the configuration and operations layers on top

blocks.title: Today's default
blocks.text: Databricks currently recommends **serverless** as the default for most new workloads, and **classic** only when you need capabilities or configuration that serverless does not support.
Say you create **classic compute** with: Driver = 8 cores / 32 GB, Workers = 4 × (8 cores / 32 GB).

DRIVER VM
               8 CPU / 32 GB
                    |
     +----------+---+------+----------+
     v          v          v          v
 WORKER 1   WORKER 2   WORKER 3   WORKER 4
  8 cores    8 cores    8 cores    8 cores
  32 GB      32 GB      32 GB      32 GB
blocks.caption: 1 driver machine + 4 worker machines = 5 cloud VMs

blocks.label: Think first: how many cloud VMs is that, and how many executor cores?
blocks.text: **5 VMs** (1 driver + 4 workers). Executor cores = 4 × 8 = **32**, not 40. Worker RAM ≈ 4 × 32 = **128 GB**. The driver is a separate coordinator, not distributed capacity.

blocks.caption: What you actually bought

blocks.title: Don't add the driver to worker capacity
blocks.text: Saying "**40 worker cores**" (32 + 8 driver cores) is the classic counting mistake. The driver's cores are **not** executor cores.

blocks.title: Head chef vs line cooks
blocks.text: The **driver** is the head chef who reads orders and assigns dishes. The workers are the cooking stations. Hiring a bigger head chef adds no extra stove.

sections.title: Driver vs Executors (Level-up)
sections.hook: The driver plans, the executors do. Mixing them up leads to wrong sizing and wrong OOM fixes.

blocks.title: Level-up from ch08
blocks.text: Ch08 already taught *driver = coordinator, worker = processing*. Here you add the **full list of driver jobs**, the **plan pipeline**, and the **one-executor-per-worker** rule.
Databricks describes the **driver** as the node that keeps the state of attached notebooks, maintains the SparkContext, interprets commands and coordinates the executors.

blocks.label: Think first: does the driver fetch all rows and start adding amounts?
blocks.text: No. The driver first builds a **plan**: Logical Plan (Aggregate ← Scan sales.orders) → Optimized Plan → Physical Plan. Then it splits the physical plan into stages/tasks that the **workers** run on the actual partitions.

Scan sales.orders          (on workers, per partition)
     |
Partial Aggregate          (sum per country, per partition)
     |
Exchange                   (shuffle by country)
     |
Final Aggregate            (combine partial sums)
blocks.caption: The physical plan of the groupBy

blocks.text: Not 100% true for every implementation detail, but **driver ≠ worker** is the right mental model and it is fundamental.

blocks.title: One executor per worker
blocks.text: In vanilla Spark, worker machines and executors can relate in complex ways. In **Databricks classic**, Databricks runs **one Spark executor per worker node** — that's why the docs use *worker* and *executor* almost interchangeably. 8 workers → normally 8 executors.

Worker 1 ── Executor 1
Worker 2 ── Executor 2
Worker 3 ── Executor 3

blocks.title: Certification trap: executors
blocks.text: "Databricks classic compute has 6 workers. How many Spark executors?" → **6**. One executor per worker. Don't add one for the driver and don't multiply by cores.

sections.title: Cores, Tasks, Partitions & Waves
sections.hook: The most useful sizing formula in Spark: tasks ÷ task slots = waves.

blocks.text: Spark uses **cores** as the basis for task parallelism: roughly **one active task per available executor core**. Databricks states a 1:1 mapping between task slots and available cores.
So an 8-core worker can usually run about **8 tasks concurrently**.
A **task** is the smallest basic execution unit of a Spark stage. Within a stage, **1 partition → 1 task**.

blocks.code:
# DataFrame with 100 partitions
df.filter("amount > 10").count()
# → this stage has ~100 tasks
blocks.caption: 100 partitions → 100 tasks

blocks.text:
4 workers × 8 cores = 32 task slots

Wave 1 → 32 tasks
Wave 2 → 32 tasks
Wave 3 → 32 tasks
Wave 4 →  4 tasks   (28 slots idle)
         ───
         100 tasks = 4 waves
blocks.caption: Tasks beyond the slot count run in waves (conceptually)

blocks.title: The formulas
blocks.text:
**Task slots** = workers × cores per worker (driver excluded).
**Waves** ≈ ceil(tasks ÷ slots), assuming similar task durations.

head: Partitions in stage
On 32 slots
Verdict
rows: Huge cluster, not enough parallel work
Fine — more partitions than cores is not a problem by itself
blocks.caption: The partition count decides how many parallel pieces of work exist

blocks.title: Big cluster, tiny parallelism
blocks.text: A 32-core cluster reading a dataset with **4 partitions** keeps 28 cores idle. Parallelism is capped by partitions, not by the size of the bill.

End-to-end: `spark.read.table("orders").groupBy("country").sum("amount")` with 64 input partitions. **Stage 1** = 64 tasks (task 1 → partition 1 … task 64 → partition 64). The groupBy causes a **shuffle**; if Spark uses 200 shuffle partitions, **Stage 2** = 200 tasks.

Stage 1: 64 input partitions  → 64 tasks
            |  shuffle (groupBy)
            v
Stage 2: 200 shuffle partitions → 200 tasks
blocks.caption: Partition count is stage-specific

blocks.title: No single partition count per job
blocks.text: **Partition count is stage-specific.** A job does not have one partition number — each stage has its own.
On 4 workers × 8 cores (32 slots): Stage 1 = 64 tasks → **2 waves**. Stage 2 = 200 tasks → 200/32 = 6.25 → **7 waves**.

blocks.title: Waves are conceptual
blocks.text: Tasks don't all take the same time. In practice **skew** can make one task run far longer than the others, so real execution isn't neat waves.

blocks.label: Exercise 2: 6 workers × 16 cores, stage with 768 partitions. How many task slots and waves?
blocks.text: Slots = 6 × 16 = **96**. Waves ≈ 768 / 96 = **8**, if all tasks have similar duration.

sections.title: Scale Up vs Scale Out & Memory per Core
sections.hook: Same total cores and RAM can still behave very differently — the shape of the cluster matters.

blocks.title: Level-up from ch08
blocks.text: Ch08 defined *scale up* (bigger machines) and *scale out* (more machines). Here you learn **why the shape changes behaviour** and the **memory-per-core** heuristic.
The **totals are identical**. Databricks uses exactly this kind of example in its sizing best practices — and the point is that equal cores ≠ equal performance.

blocks.label: Think first: A and B both have 8 GB per core. So what actually differs?
blocks.text: The **executor heap** (one 128 GB executor vs one 32 GB executor), **shuffle fan-out** (8 workers exchange blocks with more peers over the network), **fault impact** (losing 1 of 2 workers loses 50% of capacity; 1 of 8 loses 12.5%) and **local disk** per node.
**Per-task memory example**: each task needs ~10 GB of working memory. A worker with 4 cores / 16 GB runs 4 concurrent tasks.

Worker: 4 cores / 16 GB

 task1 10GB  task2 10GB  task3 10GB  task4 10GB
 └──────────────── 40 GB working set ────────┘
                     vs 16 GB RAM
                  → spill or OOM
blocks.caption: 4 × 10 GB = 40 GB potential working set in a 16 GB worker

blocks.text: A worker with 4 cores / **64 GB** has a much larger memory-per-core ratio and handles the same tasks comfortably.

blocks.title: Memory per core > raw GB
blocks.text: **Memory per core** matters more than total GB. Worker A: 4 cores / 16 GB = **4 GB/core**. Worker B: 4 cores / 32 GB = **8 GB/core**.

blocks.title: When you suspect a memory problem
blocks.text: Databricks suggests trying a **higher memory-per-core ratio** to see whether behaviour changes, and recommends **memory-optimized workers** for heavy shuffle, spill and memory-intensive workloads.

sections.title: Where Worker RAM Goes: Execution, Storage & Spill
sections.hook: A 32 GB worker never gives 32 GB to your rows — and running out of RAM usually means spill, not failure.

blocks.text: Don't imagine **32 GB worker = 32 GB available for Spark rows**. Several consumers share worker RAM.

Worker RAM
├── JVM heap
│   ├── Spark execution memory
│   ├── cached data
│   ├── JVM objects
│   └── metadata
├── off-heap / native memory
├── Python worker processes
├── Photon / native processing
└── OS / Databricks services
blocks.caption: Who eats worker memory

blocks.title: Not a simple formula
blocks.text: The exact allocation is **not** simply RAM ÷ cores. But for sizing, **memory per core** is still a useful heuristic.
Spark has **unified memory management**: execution and storage can, to some degree, share the available managed memory.

blocks.title: What interviewers want
blocks.text: You don't need every memory fraction by heart. You need this: **join / sort / groupBy can eat execution memory even if you never called `cache()`**.
**Spill**: a task must sort 20 GB but can't keep all intermediate data in RAM. Spark writes intermediate data to the **local worker disk** and keeps going.

items: Write intermediate data to local worker disk
blocks.caption: What spill is

blocks.text: The Spark UI shows spill as **Memory Bytes Spilled** and **Disk Bytes Spilled**.

blocks.title: Spill ≠ failure
blocks.text: **Spill does not mean the job is broken.** Spark is designed so operations can spill. But *huge, repeated* spill can make a workload very slow.

blocks.title: Fix direction
blocks.text: Databricks lists memory-intensive **shuffle/spill** workloads as a use case for **memory-optimized workers** — after you've ruled out skew and bad partitioning.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when the Spark UI shows spill
questions: Is this a little spill or huge, repeated spill that slows the stage?
Is the spill concentrated in one task (skew) or spread across all tasks?
Are my partitions too large because there are too few shuffle partitions?
Is a join or aggregation building a big hash table in execution memory?
Would a higher memory-per-core worker change the behaviour?

sections.title: Shuffle & the Temporary Local Disk
sections.hook: Shuffle writes to local disks and crosses the network — and none of that survives the cluster.

blocks.text: **Map-side tasks** produce shuffle output and write it as **shuffle files on each worker's local disk**. Downstream tasks then **pull** those blocks over the network.

Worker 1 local disk: shuffle files ─┐
Worker 2 local disk: shuffle files ─┼─ network ─> downstream tasks
Worker 3 local disk: shuffle files ─┘

Worker A ── shuffle blocks ── network ──> Worker B
blocks.caption: Shuffle = local disk + network

blocks.text: So heavy **shuffle** puts pressure on four resources at once:
Executors' **local disks** are used, among other things, for shuffle files, spill and caching.

blocks.label: Think first: what happens to those local files when the cluster stops?
blocks.text: The **worker VM is destroyed**. Local shuffle files, cached partitions, temp files and spill files can all be lost.

items.title: Local worker disk
points: gone when the VM is destroyed

items.title: Delta table storage
points: your tables and their transaction log

blocks.title: Local disk is not storage
blocks.text: **Local worker disk = temporary compute storage.** Never rely on cached/local data surviving; persist results as Delta tables in cloud storage.

sections.title: Driver OOM vs Executor OOM
sections.hook: Two different crashes, two different fixes — and "double the cluster" is usually the wrong first move.

blocks.text: **Example**: Workers = 20 × 64 GB, Driver = 8 GB. You run `rows = df.collect()` on a 100 GB result. The workers are fine — the **driver** collapses.

blocks.code:
rows = df.collect()   # pulls every row into driver memory
pdf = df.toPandas()   # same: materializes the data on the driver
blocks.caption: The two classic driver killers

blocks.title: Databricks' list
blocks.text: Databricks names **skew, large broadcasts, UDFs, unpartitioned windows and too few shuffle partitions** as common causes of memory failures.
**Bad reasoning**: OOM → double the cluster. **Better**: walk a diagnosis chain first.

blocks.caption: Memory debugging chain — before adding RAM

blocks.title: Mnemonic
blocks.text: **W**ise **D**octors **S**can **S**ymptoms, **J**udge **W**ounds, **P**rescribe **M**edicine → **W**hich task · **D**ominant partition · **S**kew · **S**pill · **J**oin · **W**indow · **P**artitions too few · **M**emory/core.

blocks.title: 100 workers can't split one partition
blocks.text: If the problem is **one 100 GB partition**, having 100 workers barely helps: a single task must still process those 100 GB.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when something dies with OOM
questions: Did the driver die or an executor? (Where is the error coming from?)
If the driver: did I call collect(), toPandas() or build a huge result/plan?
If an executor: which task failed, and does one partition dominate in size?
Is there skew, a big hash join or broadcast, or an unpartitioned window?
Are there too few shuffle partitions, making each partition huge?
Only then: would a higher memory-per-core worker help?

sections.title: Autoscaling From First Principles (Level-up)
sections.hook: Autoscaling adds task slots — it never adds partitions and never fixes skew.

blocks.title: Level-up from ch08
blocks.text: Ch08 covered *classic min/max workers* vs *serverless managed scaling*. Here you do the **slot math**, see **what autoscaling cannot fix**, and meet two exam traps.
Worker = 8 cores / 32 GB, **Min workers = 2**, **Max workers = 8**. Minimum capacity = 2 × 8 = **16 task slots**; maximum = 8 × 8 = **64 task slots**.

blocks.caption: Parallel task capacity can move between limits depending on the workload

blocks.title: What does NOT change
blocks.text: Worker size stays **8 cores / 32 GB each**. Autoscaling never turns "2 huge VMs" into "8 tiny VMs". It is **horizontal autoscaling**: it changes the *number* of workers.

blocks.label: Think first: a stage has 1 partition. You scale from 2 to 100 workers. How many tasks?
blocks.text: **1.** So about 1 core is busy and hundreds are idle. **Autoscaling doesn't magically create partitions.**
**Skew failure**: a stage with 100 partitions — 99 of 100 MB, one of **200 GB**. Scaling 4 → 40 workers makes the 99 small ones finish fast, but the job ends only when **the straggler** finishes.

blocks.title: Skew ≠ missing capacity
blocks.text: When one giant task dominates, the problem is **skew**, not insufficient parallel capacity. More workers just means more idle cores waiting.

blocks.label: Exercise 3: 4 workers × 8 cores, stage of 30 partitions. Autoscale to 8 workers — big speed-up?
blocks.text: No. 32 slots already run all **30 tasks** at once. At 8 workers you have 64 slots but still only 30 tasks → essentially **no gain in task parallelism**.

items.title: Serverless autoscaling
points: Databricks manages instances, capacity, scaling, runtime
serverless Jobs: automatic scaling + platform-managed Photon

blocks.title: Serverless does autoscale
blocks.text: **Serverless autoscales**, but it's usually *not* the manual `min_workers` / `max_workers` axis. You can't set min_workers=2, max_workers=10 for ordinary serverless notebook compute the classic way.

blocks.title: Certification trap: autoscaling
blocks.text: Classic autoscaling primarily changes the **number of workers**, **not the worker instance size**.

blocks.title: Certification trap: Spark dynamic allocation
blocks.text: Vanilla Spark has `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled`. Databricks explicitly lists the **dynamic-allocation properties as unsupported** on classic compute and tells you to use **Databricks autoscaling** instead.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before turning up max workers
questions: How many tasks does the slow stage actually have compared with my task slots?
Are tasks fewer than slots already (more workers = more idle cores)?
Is one straggler task dominating the stage (skew)?
Am I trying to fix this with spark.dynamicAllocation instead of Databricks autoscaling?

sections.title: Single Node, Zero Workers & Access Modes (Level-up)
sections.hook: Single node ≠ zero workers, and Dedicated ≠ faster. Two favourite exam traps.

blocks.title: Level-up from ch08
blocks.text: Ch08 introduced single/multi-node and Standard/Dedicated. New here: the **zero-workers trap**, **Auto** access mode, the **2026 UI change**, and the rule *capability, not performance*.
Classic doesn't have to mean a distributed cluster. In **Single node** mode there are no separate worker nodes — Databricks says the **driver also acts as the worker**.

blocks.title: Certification trap: zero workers
blocks.text: A **multi-node** compute with **0 workers**: can it run Spark distributed commands? **No.** Docs: without worker nodes, *non-Spark* commands run on the driver but **Spark commands fail**. If you want single-machine Spark, pick **Single Node** — a separate mode.

blocks.title: 2026 nuance: the UI changed
blocks.text: The current UI has **no separate obvious "multi-node" selector**: compute is multi-node by default and you choose **Single node** when desired. **Driver type** moved under **Advanced Performance** and defaults to **Auto**. Older tutorials and screenshots look different.

items.title: Standard
points: many users share one compute with workload isolation
Databricks' recommended mode for most workloads

items.title: Dedicated
points: assigned to a specific user or (in supported setups) a group
for RDD APIs, R, GPU, ML Runtime

items.title: Auto
points: Databricks picks Standard or Dedicated by runtime/hardware
prefers Standard; switches to Dedicated for ML Runtime, GPU or a fairly old DBR

blocks.text: **Practical rule for data engineering**: **Standard** by default. Dedicated only when you can say "I need a specific capability that Standard doesn't support".

blocks.title: Dedicated is not a performance tier
blocks.text: Don't pick **Dedicated** because it "sounds faster" or because "production is important". It's a **security/capability mode**, not a speed setting.

blocks.title: Certification trap: Standard vs Dedicated
blocks.text: Choose Dedicated only when the workload **requires** capabilities Standard can't support. **Standard** is the recommended classic access mode for most workloads.

sections.title: Pools & Spot Instances (Level-up)
sections.hook: Pools answer "where do the VMs come from?" — spot answers "how cheap can they be?"

blocks.title: Level-up from ch08
blocks.text: Ch08 explained what a pool is and pool lifecycle. Here: the **full mental model** (pool vs cluster, pool vs autoscaling, serverless vs pools) plus **spot instances**.

blocks.caption: Without a pool: every start pays the provisioning wait

blocks.text:
POOL (pre-warmed VM capacity)
├── idle VM
├── idle VM
├── idle VM
└── used VM

cluster → pool → warm instance available → attach quickly
Pool parameters (as described for the AWS implementation) include:

items.title: Pool
points: can serve more than one compute

items.title: Compute (cluster)
points: draws its nodes from the pool

blocks.text:
POOL
     ┌───────┼───────┐
     v       v       v
 Cluster A Cluster B Cluster C
Cluster wants to grow **2 → 6 workers**. The **autoscaler** decides "I need +4". The **pool** answers "here are 4 warm VMs".

blocks.title: Two different questions
blocks.text: **Autoscaler: HOW MANY?** **Pool: WHERE DO THE VMs COME FROM?** A pool never decides how many workers Spark needs.

**Serverless vs pools**: serverless makes the pool problem a **platform concern**. That's why Databricks now recommends serverless instead of pools where the workload is compatible. Serverless doesn't support user-configured instance pools.

items.title: Spot VM
points: can be reclaimed by the cloud provider

blocks.text: If a spot worker disappears, Spark can often **retry** its tasks: task lost → scheduled elsewhere. So spot is attractive for **fault-tolerant batch**, not for every workload.

blocks.title: Spot and latency-sensitive streaming
blocks.text: Current Databricks **real-time streaming mode requires spot off**, because interruptions are bad for latency-sensitive persistent processing.

blocks.title: Driver on spot?
blocks.text: You usually want the **driver** stable. Lose a worker → some tasks retry. Lose the driver → the **Spark application itself** is disrupted. Architectures separate driver reliability from worker cost optimization.

sections.title: Termination, Lifecycle & Permissions (Level-up)
sections.hook: Terminated is not deleted, and "can attach" is not "can read the data".

blocks.title: Level-up from ch08
blocks.text: Ch08 covered termination and auto-termination basics and SQL-warehouse ACLs. New here: exactly **what survives**, **jobs lifecycle**, **compute permission levels** and **serverless permission objects**.
Why? Interactive clusters **cost money even when the developer went for coffee**.
**Termination ≠ delete.** Press **Start** and a **fresh** compute is created from the saved configuration — but all ephemeral state is gone.

head: Ephemeral (lost)
Persistent (kept)
blocks.caption: Big-test answer: what disappears vs what remains

blocks.text: Jobs compute is governed by the **workload lifecycle**, not mainly by an idle timeout. Databricks generally discourages all-purpose compute for automated production jobs.

head: Compute permission
What it allows
rows: Attach a notebook and use the compute
Also change compute configuration and permissions

blocks.title: Compute ACL ≠ Unity Catalog ACL
blocks.text: You can have **CAN ATTACH TO** on the cluster and still have **SELECT prod.payroll = NO** → the query fails. Compute permissions never grant data access.

**Serverless permissions**: serverless doesn't mean everyone has access. The workspace has serverless permission objects — **Default Interactive Compute** (notebooks / Databricks Connect) and **Default Automated Compute** (Jobs / Pipelines) — with **CAN USE** and management permissions.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a query fails on a cluster I can attach to
questions: Is this a compute problem (can't attach/start) or a data problem (permission denied on a table)?
Which identity is actually running the query?
Does that identity have the Unity Catalog privileges (e.g. SELECT) on the table?
Am I confusing CAN ATTACH TO / CAN MANAGE with data access?

sections.title: Photon in the Execution Stack (Level-up)
sections.hook: Photon speeds up SQL/DataFrame operators on CPUs — not Python loops, not GPUs.

blocks.title: Level-up from ch08
blocks.text: Ch08 explained what Photon is and where it's configured. Here: where it sits in the **execution stack**, and why **UDFs** reduce its benefit.

Spark DataFrame / SQL
        |
     Catalyst
        |
  Physical Plan
        |
┌──────────────────┐
│ Photon native    │
│   or Spark JVM   │
└──────────────────┘
        |
   workers / CPU
blocks.caption: Photon is an execution engine under the physical plan

blocks.text: **Photon** is a native, vectorized engine. It's enabled in **serverless** and **SQL warehouses**; on classic all-purpose / jobs / pipelines it's configurable, and in the current UI it's **default-on**.

blocks.caption: Photon does NOT turn this into fast native execution

blocks.title: Photon is not a Python accelerator — nor a GPU
blocks.text: Photon is **CPU-native vectorized query execution**. It won't speed up arbitrary Python loops, and it has nothing to do with GPUs.

items.title: Built-in functions
points: native engine has a much bigger chance to accelerate

items.title: Opaque Python UDF
points: a black box to the optimizer

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.text: Prefer **built-in Spark SQL / DataFrame functions** wherever possible.

blocks.title: Larger driver or Photon?
blocks.text: For a **CPU-bound SQL aggregation**, **Photon / query optimization** is far more relevant than a bigger driver — the aggregation runs on the workers.

sections.title: Serverless Trade-offs & the Compute Selection Algorithm
sections.hook: Serverless removes the knobs — that's both the limitation and the benefit.

blocks.text: Databricks does **not** give you control in serverless over:

blocks.title: Limitation AND benefit
blocks.text: Losing these knobs is not only a limitation — it's the **abstraction benefit**: no node sizing, no pool tuning, no idle clusters.
**What you sacrifice: control.** Current serverless limitations include:

START
  |
Can serverless support the workload?
  ├── YES → prefer serverless
  └── NO  → classic required
              |
        Need shared general DE/SQL?
              ├── yes → Standard
              └── need R/RDD/GPU/ML Runtime?
                        → Dedicated
blocks.caption: Compute selection algorithm

blocks.text: This matches current Databricks recommendations.

blocks.label: Think first: a team needs R for analysis. Which compute?
blocks.text: Serverless has **no R** → classic required. Standard doesn't support R → **classic Dedicated**.

blocks.title: Order of the questions matters
blocks.text: Ask **"can serverless do it?"** first. Only if not, go classic, then pick **Standard** unless you need a Dedicated-only capability.

sections.title: Diagnosing Workloads: Spark UI & Bottleneck Types
sections.hook: Before buying more hardware, read the task-metric distributions and name the bottleneck.

blocks.text: **Real sizing case**: daily batch ETL, 2 TB input, operations filter → join → groupBy. Driver 8 cores/32 GB; workers 4 × (8 cores/32 GB) → 32 worker cores, 128 GB; **autoscale 4–12**.
The initial scan creates **2,000 partitions**. At 4 workers: **32** concurrent tasks. At 12 workers: **96** concurrent tasks. So the scan phase can gain a lot of parallelism.
But after the shuffle the **join stage** has 499 partitions of 2 GB and **one of 300 GB**. Scaling 4 → 12 makes the small ones finish faster, but the 300 GB task stays the bottleneck.

Spark UI, join stage:
  many tasks .......... done
  one task: huge duration
            huge shuffle read
            huge spill

Diagnosis: SKEW  — not "need 50 workers"

blocks.caption: Spark UI path for a slow stage

blocks.title: The skew signal
blocks.text: **Median task = 20 sec, max task = 15 min**, with a huge shuffle read on the max task → **strong skew signal**.

head: Bottleneck
Signals
Potential fixes
rows: CPU high, little spill, memory OK, tasks balanced
more cores, compute-optimized workers, Photon, better algorithm/query — not just more RAM
high spill, executor OOM, GC high, CPU not fully useful
higher memory/core, more partitions, remove skew, smaller broadcast, different join, memory-optimized worker
CPU low, tasks spend time reading
fix storage/file layout, too many small files, network, poor pruning, reading too much data
blocks.caption: Name the bottleneck first

blocks.title: Scaling the wrong resource
blocks.text: For an **I/O-bound** job, scaling CPU may not help. For a **CPU-bound** job, more RAM won't help.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a stage is slow
questions: Which stage is slow, and how many tasks does it have vs my slots?
Is max task duration far above the median (skew)?
Does the slowest task also have the biggest shuffle read / spill?
Is CPU high (CPU-bound), spill/GC high (memory-bound) or CPU low while reading (I/O-bound)?
Am I about to scale the resource that isn't the bottleneck?

sections.title: Hands-on: Config, Partitions, Plans & Experiments
sections.hook: Five lines of code connect compute sizing to what Spark actually executes.

blocks.code:
spark.version                                   # Spark version
spark.conf.get("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions")  # inspect a Spark config
blocks.caption: Inspect runtime and Spark config

blocks.text: Databricks documents **`spark.conf.get(...)`** as the way to inspect Spark configuration.

blocks.title: RDD access needed
blocks.text: `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()` needs **RDD access** → fine on compatible classic compute, but **not on serverless** (Spark Connect), where RDD APIs aren't supported. There, reason from the **query plan** and **Spark UI / query profile** instead.

items: A classic Databricks cluster has one Spark driver and one executor per worker.
Each worker contributes CPU cores, and Spark generally maps one task slot to each available executor core.
Partitions determine how many independent tasks a stage can expose — so adding workers only helps if the stage has enough useful parallelism.
Worker memory is used for execution, caching, native/Python processing and platform overhead; when execution data doesn't fit, Spark may spill to local worker disk.
Driver memory is separate: collect() and toPandas() can OOM the driver even when executors have huge aggregate RAM.
Classic autoscaling changes worker count between configured limits; serverless also scales, but Databricks controls the infrastructure.
Standard and Dedicated are access/capability modes, not performance tiers.
Pools accelerate provisioning of classic compute; they do not decide the worker count — autoscaling does.

blocks.label: Think first: which single number limits a stage's parallelism even on a 1,000-core cluster?
blocks.text: The stage's **partition count**. One partition → one task; tasks can't exceed partitions.

blocks.title: Next practical step
blocks.text: Open a realistic **Create Compute** form field by field and design three clusters: an **interactive development** cluster, a **production batch ETL** cluster and a **memory-heavy Spark job** — then predict their Spark UI behaviour and debug deliberately bad configurations.

debug.title: Executor OOM (or executors keep dying)
debug.symptom: A stage fails with executor out-of-memory / executor lost errors; the reflex is to double the cluster.
askYourself: Which executor and which task died — is it one task or all of them?
Does one partition dominate in size (input / shuffle read)?
Is that domination skew in the join or groupBy key?
Is there heavy spill before the crash?
Is a join building a large hash table or a large broadcast?
Is there an unpartitioned or huge window partition?
Are there too few shuffle partitions, so every partition is huge?
Only now: would a higher memory-per-core worker change the behaviour?

steps.do: Open the failed stage in the Spark UI and sort tasks by duration / shuffle read.
steps.why: Tells you whether one task or all tasks are under memory pressure.

steps.do: Compare median vs max of Input Size, Shuffle Read, Memory/Disk Spill.
steps.why: A max far above the median = skew; uniform high values = too few partitions or too little memory/core.

steps.do: Read the plan for join strategy and windows.
steps.why: BroadcastHashJoin of a big table or a window without partitionBy can blow executor memory.

steps.do: Check the shuffle partition setting.
steps.why: Too few shuffle partitions makes each one too big.

steps.do: Fix the cause (skew handling, more partitions, smaller broadcast, different join); then, if still needed, test a higher memory/core or memory-optimized worker.
steps.why: Hardware is the last lever, not the first.

debug.fix: Diagnose before scaling: remove skew, raise partition count, change join/broadcast, partition windows; then increase memory per core (memory-optimized workers) if the workload genuinely needs it.
debug.mnemonic: Wise Doctors Scan Symptoms, Judge Wounds, Prescribe Medicine (Which task · Dominant partition · Skew · Spill · Join · Window · Partitions · Memory/core)

debug.title: Driver OOM after collect() / toPandas()
debug.symptom: The notebook crashes or the driver restarts right after df.collect() or df.toPandas(), while the workers have plenty of RAM.
askYourself: Did the driver die, not an executor?
Which action pulled data to the driver — collect(), toPandas(), a huge display/result?
How big is that result compared with the driver's RAM?
Could I aggregate, filter or limit on the workers first?
Could I write the result to a Delta table instead of bringing it to the driver?
Is something else bloating the driver — huge plan, many task metadata, large local Python objects?

steps.do: Confirm the failing component is the driver.
steps.why: Driver OOM and executor OOM have different fixes.

steps.do: Find the action that materializes data on the driver.
steps.why: collect()/toPandas() move all distributed rows into one machine.

steps.do: Estimate result size vs driver memory (e.g. 100 GB result vs 8 GB driver).
steps.why: Aggregate worker RAM is irrelevant — only the driver's RAM counts here.

steps.do: Reduce on the workers (aggregate/filter/limit) or write to a table.
steps.why: Keeps the heavy work distributed.

steps.do: Only if you truly need a large driver-side result, pick a larger driver type.
steps.why: Driver size is the last lever.

debug.fix: Keep results distributed (aggregate, filter, write to Delta); bring only small results to the driver; size the driver up only when a large driver-side result is genuinely required.
debug.mnemonic: Driver = desk, not warehouse: never pour the warehouse onto the desk.

debug.title: More workers, no speed-up (autoscaling doesn't help)
debug.symptom: You raised max workers (or autoscaling added nodes) but the slow stage takes just as long; most cores are idle.
askYourself: How many tasks does the slow stage have?
How many task slots did I have before scaling (workers × cores)?
Are tasks ≤ slots already, so new workers can only sit idle?
Does the stage have 1 or very few partitions (coalesce(1), single file, tiny shuffle)?
Is one straggler task dominating instead (skew)?
Should I repartition / raise shuffle partitions instead of adding workers?

steps.do: Count the tasks of the slow stage in the Spark UI.
steps.why: Parallelism is capped by partitions: 1 partition → 1 task.

steps.do: Compute slots = workers × cores and compare with the task count.
steps.why: 30 tasks on 32 slots already run in one wave; 64 slots change nothing.

steps.do: Check for coalesce(1) or a single-partition source.
steps.why: A collapsed partition count kills parallelism.

steps.do: Increase useful parallelism (repartition, more shuffle partitions) or fix skew.
steps.why: Creates tasks the extra cores can actually run.

rootCauses: too few partitions / tasks for the slots
debug.fix: Match partitions to slots (repartition / shuffle partitions) or fix skew; autoscaling only adds slots, never partitions.
debug.mnemonic: Count TASKS before you count WORKERS.

debug.title: One straggler task (data skew)
debug.symptom: 99% of tasks finish in seconds; one runs for minutes with huge shuffle read and spill. Scaling out barely changes job time.
askYourself: In the stage's task metrics, how far is the max duration from the median?
Does the slowest task also have the largest shuffle read / input size / records?
Does that task show huge memory or disk spill?
Which key is it partitioned by (join key, groupBy key)?
Would more workers or more RAM actually redistribute that data? (No.)

steps.do: Spark UI → Stages → open the slow stage → task metrics.
steps.why: Distributions reveal skew, averages hide it.

steps.do: Compare Duration, Shuffle Read, Records, Spill: median vs max.
steps.why: median 20 s vs max 15 min with huge shuffle read = strong skew signal.

steps.do: Identify the skewed key in the join/groupBy.
steps.why: Skew is a data-distribution problem.

steps.do: Address the distribution (skew handling) rather than scaling.
steps.why: More memory may reduce spill/failure but doesn't redistribute data.

rootCauses: one key holds a huge share of the rows (e.g. 300 GB partition among 2 GB ones)
bad join on a skewed key
debug.fix: Treat it as skew: fix the data distribution for the skewed key; don't buy 50 workers or double RAM as a cure.
debug.mnemonic: Median vs Max: a big gap means a skewed map.

debug.title: Huge disk spill / memory-bound slow stage
debug.symptom: The stage is very slow; Spark UI shows large Memory Bytes Spilled and Disk Bytes Spilled, high GC time, but no failure.
askYourself: Is the spill huge and repeated, or a small normal amount?
Is spill concentrated in a few tasks (skew) or spread over all (memory pressure)?
Are partitions too large because shuffle partitions are too few?
Is a join/aggregation building big hash tables (execution memory)?
What is my memory per core, and would a memory-optimized worker change behaviour?

steps.do: Check spill per task in the stage's task metrics.
steps.why: Separates skew from general memory pressure.

steps.do: Check partition size and the shuffle partition count.
steps.why: Too-large partitions force spill.

steps.do: Inspect the join strategy in the plan.
steps.why: A bad join can explode execution memory.

steps.do: Then test higher memory per core / memory-optimized workers.
steps.why: Databricks recommends them for memory-intensive shuffle/spill workloads.

debug.fix: Spill isn't failure: fix partition size/skew/join first; if the workload really is memory-intensive, use higher memory/core or memory-optimized workers.
debug.mnemonic: Spill = symptom, not sentence: find out WHY it spills.

debug.title: Slow job: which bottleneck is it? (CPU / memory / I/O)
debug.symptom: A job is slow but not failing; someone proposes "just add more workers/RAM".
askYourself: Is CPU high with little spill and balanced tasks? (CPU-bound)
Is spill high, GC high, maybe executor OOM, while CPU isn't doing useful work? (memory-bound)
Is CPU low while tasks spend their time reading? (I/O-bound)
Are there few extreme stragglers? (skew, not capacity)
Does the fix I'm proposing target that resource?

steps.do: Look at cluster metrics (CPU) and Spark UI task metrics (spill, GC, input).
steps.why: Each bottleneck has a different fingerprint.

steps.do: CPU-bound → more/faster cores, compute-optimized workers, Photon, better query.
steps.why: More RAM won't help a CPU-bound job.

steps.do: Memory-bound → higher memory/core, more partitions, remove skew, smaller broadcast, different join.
steps.why: Targets memory pressure.

steps.do: I/O-bound → fix file layout, small files, pruning, read less data.
steps.why: Scaling CPU may not help I/O.

rootCauses: I/O: small files, poor pruning, reading too much, network
debug.fix: Name the bottleneck first, then apply the matching row of the best-practice matrix.
debug.mnemonic: C-M-I: CPU hot? Memory spilling? I/O waiting?

debug.title: Spark commands fail on a cluster with 0 workers
debug.symptom: A multi-node compute was configured with 0 workers; plain Python works in the notebook, but every Spark command fails.
askYourself: Is this a multi-node compute with zero workers, or a real Single Node compute?
Do non-Spark commands work while Spark commands fail?
Do I actually need distributed workers, or just single-machine Spark?

steps.do: Check the compute configuration: worker count and node mode.
steps.why: Docs: without workers, non-Spark commands run on the driver but Spark commands fail.

steps.do: For single-machine Spark, recreate/edit as Single node.
steps.why: Single Node is a separate mode where the driver also acts as worker.

steps.do: For distributed work, set ≥ 1 worker (or autoscaling).
steps.why: Spark needs executors on workers in multi-node mode.

rootCauses: multi-node compute with zero workers is not the same as Single node mode
debug.fix: Use Single node mode for single-machine Spark, or add workers to multi-node compute.

debug.title: Query fails although I can attach to the cluster
debug.symptom: Notebook attaches fine (CAN ATTACH TO), but SELECT on prod.payroll fails with a permission error.
askYourself: Is this a compute permission problem or a data permission problem?
Which identity is running the query?
Does that identity have Unity Catalog SELECT on the table?
Am I assuming CAN ATTACH TO / CAN MANAGE grants data access?

steps.do: Separate the two gates: compute ACL vs Unity Catalog ACL.
steps.why: Compute ACL ≠ UC ACL.

steps.do: Check the UC grants on the table for the running identity.
steps.why: Data access is granted only in Unity Catalog.

steps.do: Request the needed UC privilege (or use an allowed table).
steps.why: No compute permission level can fix a data permission.

rootCauses: missing Unity Catalog privilege on the table
confusing compute ACL with data ACL
debug.fix: Get the correct Unity Catalog privilege; compute permissions (CAN ATTACH TO / RESTART / MANAGE) never grant data access.

debug.title: Cluster takes too long to start / idle cost too high
debug.symptom: Every classic cluster start waits several minutes for VMs; or interactive clusters run up costs while idle.
askYourself: Is the wait in VM provisioning (cloud) rather than in Spark itself?
Can this workload run on serverless (startup becomes a platform concern)?
If classic is required, would a pool with warm idle instances help?
Is the cost from idle interactive clusters with no or long auto-termination?

steps.do: Check whether serverless supports the workload.
steps.why: Databricks recommends serverless instead of pools where compatible.

steps.do: If classic: attach the compute to an instance pool (min idle instances, max capacity, idle auto termination).
steps.why: Warm VMs skip the provisioning wait.

steps.do: For idle cost: set auto-termination on all-purpose clusters; use jobs compute for automation.
steps.why: Interactive clusters cost money even while idle.

debug.fix: Long startup → serverless or pool. Idle interactive cost → auto-termination (and jobs compute for production).
debug.mnemonic: Slow start → Serverless or Spare (pool) VMs.

debug.title: getNumPartitions / RDD code fails on serverless
debug.symptom: df.rdd.getNumPartitions() (or other RDD code) raises an error on serverless notebook compute.
askYourself: Am I on serverless (Spark Connect), where RDD APIs aren't supported?
Can I get the information from the query plan or the Spark UI / query profile instead?
Do I truly need RDD APIs — if so, does that require classic (Dedicated) compute?

steps.do: Confirm the compute type.
steps.why: Serverless supports Spark Connect APIs only; no RDD APIs.

steps.do: Use the plan instead.
steps.why: Exchange hashpartitioning(..., N) shows shuffle partitioning.

steps.do: If RDD APIs are mandatory, move to compatible classic compute (Dedicated if Standard can't support it).
steps.why: Selection algorithm: serverless can't → classic.

rootCauses: RDD APIs are unsupported on serverless (Spark Connect)
debug.fix: Reason from explain/Spark UI/query profile on serverless; use compatible classic compute when RDD access is required.
debug.mnemonic: Serverless speaks Spark Connect, not RDD.

debug.title: spark.dynamicAllocation settings do nothing on Databricks
debug.symptom: You set spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true on a classic cluster (vanilla Spark habit) and executors don't scale as expected.
askYourself: Am I applying a vanilla-Spark property that Databricks lists as unsupported?
Is Databricks autoscaling (min/max workers) configured instead?
On serverless, am I trying to control scaling that the platform manages?

steps.do: Remove the dynamic-allocation properties.
steps.why: Databricks lists them as unsupported on classic compute.

steps.do: Enable Databricks autoscaling with min/max workers.
steps.why: That is Databricks' supported scaling mechanism.

debug.fix: Use Databricks autoscaling (classic min/max workers) or serverless managed scaling, never spark.dynamicAllocation.
debug.mnemonic: On Databricks, the autoscaler allocates — not Spark.

pitfalls.title: Counting driver cores as worker cores
pitfalls.text: Driver 4 cores + 10 × 8-core workers is 80 worker cores, not 84.
pitfalls.fix: Task slots = workers × cores per worker; exclude the driver.

pitfalls.title: Expecting more than one executor per worker
pitfalls.text: In Databricks classic there is one executor per worker node; 6 workers → 6 executors.
pitfalls.fix: Executors = workers (classic).

pitfalls.title: One partition count per job
pitfalls.text: Partition count is stage-specific: e.g. 64 input partitions, then 200 shuffle partitions.
pitfalls.fix: Reason stage by stage.

pitfalls.title: Huge cluster, few partitions
pitfalls.text: 4 partitions on 32 cores leaves 28 cores idle.
pitfalls.fix: Raise useful parallelism (repartition / shuffle partitions) before adding workers.

pitfalls.title: Too many tiny partitions
pitfalls.text: 1,000,000 tiny tasks make scheduling/startup overhead dominate useful work.
pitfalls.fix: Aim for reasonably sized partitions; coalesce when there are far too many.

pitfalls.title: Equal totals = equal performance
pitfalls.text: 2×16-core/128 GB and 8×4-core/32 GB both total 32 cores/256 GB but differ in heap, shuffle fan-out, fault impact, local disk.
pitfalls.fix: Look at shape and memory per core, not just totals.

pitfalls.title: Looking only at total GB
pitfalls.text: 4 concurrent 10 GB tasks on a 16 GB worker spill or OOM.
pitfalls.fix: Check memory per core (e.g. 4 vs 8 GB/core).

pitfalls.title: Assuming worker RAM = row memory
pitfalls.text: Worker RAM is shared by JVM heap (execution, cache, objects, metadata), off-heap, Python workers, Photon, OS/services.
pitfalls.fix: Use memory per core as a heuristic, not RAM/cores as an exact formula.

pitfalls.title: No cache() = no memory pressure
pitfalls.text: Joins, sorts and groupBys consume execution memory even without cache().
pitfalls.fix: Remember execution memory vs storage memory.

pitfalls.title: Treating spill as failure
pitfalls.text: Spill is a normal mechanism; only huge repeated spill is a performance problem.
pitfalls.fix: Investigate partition size, skew, joins, shuffle partitions.

pitfalls.title: Treating local disk as persistent
pitfalls.text: Shuffle, spill, cache and temp files on worker disks vanish with the VM.
pitfalls.fix: Persist results to Delta tables in cloud storage.

pitfalls.title: OOM → double the cluster
pitfalls.text: One 100 GB partition stays one task even with 100 workers.
pitfalls.fix: Walk the memory debugging chain first.

pitfalls.title: collect()/toPandas() on big data
pitfalls.text: Materializes everything on the driver; driver OOM even with huge worker RAM.
pitfalls.fix: Aggregate/filter on workers or write to a table.

pitfalls.title: Autoscaling to fix low parallelism or skew
pitfalls.text: Autoscaling adds slots, not partitions; a 1-partition stage stays 1 task; a straggler stays a straggler.
pitfalls.fix: Fix partitioning or skew.

pitfalls.title: Autoscaling changes worker size
pitfalls.text: Classic autoscaling changes worker count only; the instance type stays the same.
pitfalls.fix: Horizontal scaling only; choose a bigger worker type explicitly for scale-up.

pitfalls.title: Using spark.dynamicAllocation on Databricks
pitfalls.text: Databricks lists dynamic-allocation properties as unsupported on classic.
pitfalls.fix: Use Databricks autoscaling.

pitfalls.title: Expecting classic min/max workers on serverless notebooks
pitfalls.text: Serverless scales, but not via min_workers/max_workers.
pitfalls.fix: Accept platform-managed scaling or use classic if you need that control.

pitfalls.title: Multi-node with 0 workers
pitfalls.text: Non-Spark commands work on the driver, Spark commands fail.
pitfalls.fix: Use Single node mode for single-machine Spark.

pitfalls.title: Dedicated for 'important' production
pitfalls.text: Dedicated is a security/capability mode, not a performance tier.
pitfalls.fix: Standard by default; Dedicated only for R/RDD/GPU/ML Runtime/privileged needs.

pitfalls.title: Reading 'Auto' access mode as a third model
pitfalls.text: Auto just lets Databricks choose Standard or Dedicated.
pitfalls.fix: Know it prefers Standard and switches to Dedicated for ML Runtime, GPU, old DBR.

pitfalls.title: Thinking a pool decides worker count
pitfalls.text: Autoscaler decides HOW MANY; pool decides WHERE VMs come from.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the two roles separate.

pitfalls.title: Driver on spot
pitfalls.text: Losing the driver disrupts the whole Spark application; losing a worker only retries tasks.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the driver on stable capacity; use spot for workers in fault-tolerant batch.

pitfalls.title: Spot for latency-sensitive streaming
pitfalls.text: Real-time streaming mode requires spot off.
pitfalls.fix: Use on-demand for latency-sensitive persistent processing.

pitfalls.title: Termination = deletion
pitfalls.text: Termination destroys VMs and ephemeral state but keeps the configuration and permissions.
pitfalls.fix: Press Start to recreate; persist data in Delta.

pitfalls.title: Compute ACL = data access
pitfalls.text: CAN ATTACH TO doesn't grant SELECT on prod.payroll.
pitfalls.fix: Grant Unity Catalog privileges separately.

pitfalls.title: Photon = GPU / Python accelerator
pitfalls.text: Photon is CPU-native vectorized SQL/DataFrame execution; Python loops and opaque UDFs gain little.
pitfalls.fix: Prefer built-in functions; Photon for scans/joins/aggregations.

pitfalls.title: Bigger driver for CPU-bound aggregations
pitfalls.text: Aggregations run on workers; driver size doesn't help.
pitfalls.fix: Photon / query optimization / more cores.

pitfalls.title: getNumPartitions() on serverless
pitfalls.text: RDD APIs aren't supported on serverless (Spark Connect).
pitfalls.fix: Use explain / Spark UI / query profile.

pitfalls.title: coalesce(1) collapses parallelism
pitfalls.text: One partition → one task; most cores idle.
pitfalls.fix: Coalesce moderately; repartition when you need more parallelism.

pitfalls.title: Old UI screenshots
pitfalls.text: The 2026 UI has no explicit multi-node selector and moved driver type under Advanced Performance (default Auto).
pitfalls.fix: Expect multi-node by default; choose Single node explicitly.

exercises.q: Exercise 1 from the source. Driver: 4 cores / 16 GB. Workers: 10 × (8 cores / 32 GB). How many **worker cores** are there?
exercises.explain: 10 × 8 = **80** worker cores. Not 84: the driver's 4 cores are coordination capacity, not worker execution capacity. Only worker cores become task slots.

exercises.q: Same compute (driver 4c/16GB + 10 workers of 8c/32GB). How many **cloud VMs** are you paying for?
exercises.explain: 1 driver VM + 10 worker VMs = **11** VMs. The driver doesn't add task slots, but it is still a machine you pay for — every node is a VM.

exercises.q: Driver: 8 cores / 32 GB. Workers: 4 × (8 cores / 32 GB). Which statement is correct?
exercises.explain: Executors only live on workers: 4 × 8 = 32 cores and 4 × 32 = 128 GB. The tempting 40 cores / 160 GB adds the driver, which is a separate coordinator. There are 5 VMs (driver included), not 4.
options: 40 executor cores and 160 GB worker RAM
32 executor cores and 128 GB worker RAM
why: Adds the driver's 8 cores and 32 GB — classic mistake.
Correct: only workers count as distributed capacity.
Core count is right, but there are 5 VMs (the driver is a VM too).
VM count right, core count wrong (driver cores added).

exercises.q: Driver: 16 cores / 128 GB. Workers: 6 × (16 cores / 64 GB). How many **GB of worker RAM** in total?
exercises.explain: 6 × 64 = **384 GB**. The driver's 128 GB is not part of the distributed worker memory — it serves planning, results and notebook state.

exercises.q: Phase 1 builds from the lowest level up. Put the execution hierarchy in the order the source teaches it (lowest → most abstract).
exercises.explain: VM → Driver/Worker → Executor → Core → Task → Partition → Stage → Job. Machines host the driver/workers, workers host executors, executor cores run tasks, each task processes a partition, tasks form stages, stages form a job.

exercises.q: Databricks currently recommends classic compute as the default for most new workloads and serverless only for special cases.
exercises.explain: False — it's the other way round. Databricks recommends **serverless** as the default for most new workloads, and classic when you need capabilities or configuration that serverless doesn't support.

exercises.q: Match each term to its definition.
exercises.explain: The driver coordinates, the executor is the process on a worker, a task is the smallest unit of a stage, a partition is the chunk of data a task processes, and a stage is a group of tasks between shuffles.
pairs: Spark process on a worker that runs tasks
Smallest basic execution unit of a stage
Chunk of data processed by one task

exercises.model: A classic Databricks cluster has one driver and one executor per worker. Each worker contributes cores and Spark maps one task slot per executor core. Partitions determine how many tasks a stage exposes, so adding workers only helps with enough useful parallelism. Worker memory serves execution, caching, native/Python processing and platform overhead; when execution data doesn't fit, Spark spills to local disk. Driver memory is separate, so collect()/toPandas() can OOM the driver even with huge executor RAM. Classic autoscaling changes worker count within limits; serverless also scales but Databricks controls the infrastructure. Standard and Dedicated are access/capability modes, not performance tiers, and pools speed up provisioning but don't decide worker count.

exercises.model: (1) Interactive dev: all-purpose, Standard access mode, small autoscaling range (or single node for tiny data), short auto-termination, optionally a pool for fast start; expect short stages and idle periods. (2) Production batch ETL: jobs compute (or serverless jobs if supported), Standard, autoscaling sized to the scan's partitions, Photon on, spot workers but a stable driver; expect a wide scan stage with many waves and shuffle stages sized by shuffle partitions — watch for stragglers. (3) Memory-heavy job: memory-optimized workers with high GB/core, enough shuffle partitions, skew checks; expect spill metrics and GC time to be the things to monitor, and OOM if memory per core is too low.
rubric: Dev: all-purpose + auto-termination (+pool/single node)
Batch: jobs compute/serverless, autoscaling, spot workers + stable driver
Memory-heavy: memory-optimized / high GB per core, partitions
Predicts Spark UI signals (waves, stragglers, spill/GC)
